extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, courts, and enforcement personnel determining FLSA employee vs. independent contractor status
extracted.subtask_short: FLSA employee vs independent contractor analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the FLSA's economic reality test to determine whether a worker is an employee (economically dependent) or an independent contractor (in business for themself), including six core factors and related application rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate inquiry: economic dependence (economic reality test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker is economically dependent on an alleged employer who 'suffers or permits' the work, or whether the worker is in business for themself. The focus is on 'economic dependence' as the 'ultimate concept' of the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination must be made under the Act's definitions and courts' expansive reading; ask whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer. The analysis examines the 'circumstances of the whole activity' and is intended to sweep more broadly than common-law tests. Only a worker who 'is instead in business for himself' is an independent contractor. Outcomes are fact-specific and may vary even among workers in the same profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances (no single controlling factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test; no single factor is controlling or dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors are 'aids—tools to be used to gauge the degree of dependence' and must be analyzed together. The analysis cannot be conducted as a scorecard or checklist; courts admonish against mechanical application. Different factors may be more probative depending on case facts; overlap among facts is expected and permissible. The outcome depends on the whole activity, not isolated factors ("the outcome of the analysis does not depend on isolated factors but rather upon the circumstances of the whole activity").

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss depending on managerial skill (§795.110(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker exercises managerial skill that affects the worker's economic success or failure in performing the work. If a worker has no opportunity for a profit or loss, that suggests employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonexclusive list of potentially relevant facts: whether the worker determines or can meaningfully negotiate the charge or pay for the work; whether the worker accepts or declines jobs or chooses the order/time of jobs; whether the worker engages in marketing/advertising or other efforts to expand their business or secure more work; whether the worker makes decisions to hire others, purchase materials and equipment, and/or rent space. The decision to work more hours or take more jobs (when employer controls assignments or pay is hourly/flat per job) generally does not reflect managerial skill. Investment is considered a separate factor. The Department rejects treating mere technical proficiency as managerial skill, though technical skill that is the product of managerial decisions can be probative. Fines, penalties, or chargebacks may indicate dependence depending on context. The list is nonexclusive and no single fact is dispositive; industry-specific circumstances may affect how these facts are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of control exercised by the employer over the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control includes scheduling, supervision, price-setting, and restrictions on the worker's ability to work for others. The Department provides detailed discussion of how scheduling, supervision, price-setting, and the ability to work for others should be considered. Degree of control is one of the core factors courts and the Department analyze in assessing economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in facilities (investment factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The worker's investment in facilities and equipment, considered separately from opportunity for profit or loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the investment is capital or entrepreneurial in nature and consider the worker's investments relative to the employer's investments. The investment factor was returned to being a separate factor (unlike the 2021 rule which folded it into profit-or-loss), and its application assesses whether the worker has business-like investments that indicate independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill required in the claimed independent operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill required to perform the work, as it relates to claimed independent operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts sometimes treat skill together with business-like initiative. The Department cautions that technical proficiency alone (e.g., ability to complete a job) is not the type of managerial skill indicating independent contractor status under the profit-or-loss factor; however, whether skill reflects managerial decisions that affect the business overall can be probative. The factor should be considered in the context of economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The permanency or duration of the relationship between the worker and the alleged employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanency of relation is an historically identified factor (from Silk) and is considered as part of the overall totality analysis. Longer-standing, ongoing relationships may indicate employee status, but permanence is not dispositive and must be weighed with other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the work is an integral part of the employer's business (integrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker's services are an integral part of the employer's business operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly all federal courts consider integrality as a factor; the Department returns the 'integral' factor to its longstanding departmental and judicial interpretation rather than the 'integrated unit of production' approach in the 2021 rule. Integrality may be highly probative in some cases, but the Fifth Circuit sometimes assesses it as an additional relevant factor rather than an enumerated one. Consider whether the worker's duties are part of the core business rather than peripheral or independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No predetermined weighting; avoid mechanistic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assign predetermined weights to factors or create mechanistic rules for weighing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding mechanistic weighting would be contrary to judicial precedent and would limit the test's flexibility. The totality approach requires considering all relevant factors without immutable weighting; this allows the test to apply across many occupations and industries. Using a formulaic or rote analysis that isolates each factor is contrary to case law and diminishes the utility of the economic reality test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' expressed intent or contractual labels are not dispositive / FLSA rights nonwaivable
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties' expressed intention that a worker is an independent contractor does not control the statutory determination, and FLSA rights cannot be waived by contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects using the expressed intention of the parties as a threshold criterion for economic dependence. The Supreme Court has emphasized that FLSA protections are nonwaivable due to unequal bargaining power, Congress's intent to create a uniform national policy, and the Act's role in preventing unfair methods of competition. Therefore, contractual labels or agreements cannot override the statutory analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to account for industry-specific facts without carve-outs
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation is intended to be a generally applicable standard across industries rather than containing industry-specific exemptions or carve-outs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to provide industry-wide exemptions; the rule is designed to apply broadly and will allow for additional subregulatory guidance after the rule's effective date. Industry-specific facts (e.g., regulatory constraints that limit hiring or pricing) can be probative under the factors but do not automatically determine the outcome. The nonexclusive lists of facts under each factor are illustrative and not exhaustive.
